context.problemStatement:
Implement the `Lambda` case of `eval`. An anonymous function `fn(x) { ... }`
evaluates to a function value. Nothing in its body is evaluated until it is
called, so this case never returns an error. Build a `VFunc(UserFn(...))` whose
name is `"lambda"` (used in error messages) and whose parent is the environment
in which this function was *defined*, not the one in which it will be called. This
is what lets a function use the names around it, even after the call that created it
has returned.

```
// In eval:
    Lambda(params, body) ->
      // YOUR CODE HERE (replace the code below)
      Error(errors.NotImplemented(
        "Lambda("
        <> string.inspect(params)
        <> ", "
        <> string.inspect(body)
        <> ")",
      ))
```

Run the tests:

```
gleam test -- q8
```

targets.claim: Student can explain why their Lambda case never returns an error even when the body of the anonymous function uses an unbound name, and when such an error would appear instead.

probes.question: In your `Lambda` case, why does evaluating an anonymous function whose `body` contains an unbound variable not produce an error right away, and when would that error actually be raised?
probes.reason: Tests whether the student understands that lambda creation defers evaluation of the body until call time, preventing immediate evaluation errors.

probes.question: If we evaluate `Lambda(["x"], Var("undefined_var"))`, what does your `eval` return, and what needs to happen to trigger an error for `undefined_var`?
probes.reason: Uses a concrete expression to probe why lambda construction succeeds and what subsequent step causes the inner error to surface.

content: In your `Lambda` case, why does evaluating an anonymous function whose `body` contains an unbound variable not produce an error right away, and when would that error actually be raised?
lambda only returns ok, so it can't return an error.

reason: The student correctly noticed that the Lambda case returns Ok directly, but did not explain why (that the body is not evaluated at definition time) nor when the error would actually appear (at call/application time).

content: Ok, but why is it safe to return `Ok` immediately without checking the `body`, and at what point would an error in `body` actually be raised?
the check happens in fn apply

reason: The student correctly identified where the check/execution actually happens (`apply`), answering when the error would be raised. However, they haven't explicitly stated that the body is not evaluated at definition time.

content: Ok, but why doesn't evaluating the `Lambda` itself evaluate the expressions inside `body` right away?

reason: The student explained across their turns that evaluating a lambda just packages the function, that the body is evaluated during function call/application (`apply`), and that the body only runs when called, completing the full claim.
